children.title: Ambient Matrix Dimension
children.top_down_role: Global matrix-size regimes affecting storage and dense linear algebra.

assumptions_latex: The SDP has a matrix variable \(X\in\mathbb S^n\).
Matrices are stored through their independent symmetric entries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The ambient PSD dimension is \(n\), and an unrestricted symmetric iterate contains \(n(n+1)/2\) independent scalars.

notation.meaning: space of real symmetric matrices of order n

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matrix-order scale for a single PSD cone before structural decomposition.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an SDP whose positive-semidefinite variable belongs to \(\mathbb S_+^n\), the ambient matrix dimension is the order \(n\). The associated vector-space dimension is \(\dim(\mathbb S^n)=n(n+1)/2\). Thus, absent sparsity, low-rank, symmetry, or block representations, storing one symmetric primal or dual matrix requires \(n(n+1)/2\) scalar locations, while dense matrix operations act on an \(n\times n\) array.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The ambient dimension is the PSD matrix order n; a dense symmetric matrix of that order has n(n+1)/2 independent entries.
knowledge_statements.title: Ambient Matrix Dimension

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86
source_witnesses.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

children.title: PSD-Block Dimensions
children.top_down_role: Individual semidefinite block sizes governing cone-kernel cost.

assumptions_latex: The cone is represented as a product \(K=\prod_{k=1}^q\mathbb S_+^{n_k}\).
Each PSD block is stored independently.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The PSD-block dimension profile is \((n_1,\ldots,n_q)\), with \(\dim K=\sum_{k=1}^q n_k(n_k+1)/2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension profile for an explicit product of PSD cones.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the semidefinite cone be represented by \(K=\mathbb S_+^{n_1}\times\cdots\times\mathbb S_+^{n_q}\). Its PSD-block dimensions are the ordered tuple \((n_1,\ldots,n_q)\), or the corresponding multiset when block order is immaterial. The largest spectral subproblem has order \(n_{\max}=\max_{1\leq k\leq q}n_k\), and the total number of independent scalar coordinates is \(d_K=\sum_{k=1}^q n_k(n_k+1)/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: PSD-block dimensions list the orders of all product-cone blocks and determine both the largest block and total symmetric-coordinate count.
knowledge_statements.title: PSD-Block Dimensions

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86
source_witnesses.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

children.title: PSD-Block Size Distribution
children.top_down_role: Uniform, skewed, and dominant-block profiles across product cones.

assumptions_latex: The PSD cone has block orders \(n_1,\ldots,n_q\) with \(q\geq1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The block-size distribution is \(\mu_q=q^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^q\delta_{n_k}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Empirical distribution of block orders, not coordinate-weighted block mass.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For PSD-block orders \(n_1,\ldots,n_q\), the unweighted block-size distribution is the empirical probability measure \(\mu_q=q^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^q\delta_{n_k}\). Equivalently, its mass function is \(p(s)=q^{-1}|\{k:n_k=s\}|\) for positive integers \(s\). It determines block-count summaries such as quantiles and \(q^{-1}\sum_k n_k\), but not the coordinate-weighted distribution unless weights proportional to \(n_k(n_k+1)/2\) are introduced explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The block-size distribution is the empirical distribution of PSD block orders; coordinate-weighted summaries require separate symmetric-dimension weights.
knowledge_statements.title: PSD-Block Size Distribution

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86
source_witnesses.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The empirical measure is mathematically coherent, but it is a particular unweighted convention rather than an intrinsic or uniquely standard meaning of block-size distribution. The cited general structure-exploitation section does not reliably establish this exact convention or its coordinate-weighted contrast.

children.title: Constraint-System Scale
children.top_down_role: Constraint counts, dependencies, and operator dimensions relevant to execution cost.

assumptions_latex: The equality constraints are \(\mathcal A(X)=b\) with \(\mathcal A:\mathbb S^n\to\mathbb R^m\).
The matrices \(A_i\) represent \((\mathcal A(X))_i=\langle A_i,X\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Constraint-system scale is described by \(m\), \(\operatorname{rank}\mathcal A\), and \(\operatorname{nnz}(\mathcal A)=\sum_{i=1}^m\operatorname{nnz}(A_i)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic and sparsity scale of the SDP equality operator.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For constraints \(\langle A_i,X\rangle=b_i\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), the constraint-system scale comprises the listed count \(m\), the effective count \(r=\operatorname{rank}\mathcal A\), and the coefficient-storage count \(s_{\mathcal A}=\sum_{i=1}^m\operatorname{nnz}(A_i)\) under a fixed symmetric-storage convention. Redundant constraints can make \(r<m\); therefore \(m\) measures the presented system while \(r\) measures its independent linear dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constraint scale records the listed and independent constraint counts together with the nonzero count of the coefficient operator.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-System Scale

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86
source_witnesses.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

children.title: Schur-System Dimension
children.top_down_role: Reduced-system size regimes arising in second-order computation.

assumptions_latex: A Newton-type SDP method eliminates matrix directions and retains \(m\) linearly independent equality multipliers.
No additional auxiliary variables are included in the reduced system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Schur-complement system has dimension \(m\times m\); before redundancy removal its dimension is the listed constraint count.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical constraint-space Schur complement in a primal-dual Newton step.

source_refs.locator: 9.5 Schur's Algorithm p. 419
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a primal-dual Newton formulation that eliminates the matrix search direction, one scalar unknown remains for each independent equality multiplier. Hence the constraint-space Schur equation is \(H\Delta y=r\) with \(H\in\mathbb S^m\), so its dimension is \(m\). If the presented operator has rank \(r_{\mathcal A}<m\), eliminating redundant constraints reduces the effective Schur dimension to \(r_{\mathcal A}\). Additional reformulation variables change this count and must be reported separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminating matrix directions produces a Schur system whose order equals the number of independent equality constraints, unless a reformulation adds variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Schur-System Dimension

source_witnesses.locator: 9.5 Schur's Algorithm p. 419
source_witnesses.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dimension claim depends on the precise primal-dual elimination and treatment of redundant constraints. The cited locator titled “Schur's Algorithm” does not reliably establish the stated SDP Newton-system formulation, so the hypotheses and conclusion cannot be validated from the supplied evidence.

children.title: Schur-System Density
children.top_down_role: Sparsity loss and dense-coupling regimes in reduced systems.

assumptions_latex: The Schur matrix \(H\in\mathbb S^m\) is formed under a fixed structural-zero convention.
Numerical cancellation is not classified as structural sparsity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Its full-storage density is \(\rho(H)=\operatorname{nnz}(H)/m^2\), with \(0\leq\rho(H)\leq1\).

notation.meaning: number of structurally nonzero stored entries

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural density of the constraint-space Schur matrix.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a Schur-complement matrix \(H\in\mathbb S^m\), define the full-storage structural density by \(\rho(H)=\operatorname{nnz}(H)/m^2\). If only the upper triangle is counted, the equivalent convention is \(\rho_\triangle(H)=\operatorname{nnz}_\triangle(H)/(m(m+1)/2)\). A density report must specify the convention and distinguish structurally permitted entries from entries that happen to vanish numerically. Dense Schur factorization becomes relevant as \(\rho(H)\) approaches one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Schur density is the fraction of structurally nonzero matrix positions, with the full-matrix or triangular counting convention stated explicitly.
knowledge_statements.title: Schur-System Density

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86
source_witnesses.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

assumptions_latex: PSD projections or scaling operations require spectral decompositions of dense blocks of orders \(n_1,\ldots,n_q\).
Classical dense eigensolvers are used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The spectral work is \(\Theta(\sum_{k=1}^q n_k^3)\) and eigenvector storage is \(\Theta(\sum_{k=1}^q n_k^2)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dense blockwise eigendecomposition cost; iterative partial-spectrum methods are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose one iteration computes a complete eigendecomposition of every dense PSD block of order \(n_k\). In the classical dense arithmetic model, the total spectral arithmetic cost is \(\Theta(\sum_{k=1}^q n_k^3)\), and storing all eigenvector matrices costs \(\Theta(\sum_{k=1}^q n_k^2)\) scalars. For one unpartitioned block this becomes \(\Theta(n^3)\) work and \(\Theta(n^2)\) storage, explaining why the largest blocks can dominate an iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complete dense eigendecompositions cost cubically in each PSD block order and require quadratic eigenvector storage, so large blocks dominate.
knowledge_statements.title: Spectral-Computation Bottleneck

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dense complete-eigendecomposition bounds are standard and the complexity-bound kind fits the bottleneck container, but no inspectable source is supplied for the exact arithmetic and storage claims.

children.title: Iterate Storage Footprint
children.top_down_role: Memory pressure from primal, dual, slack, and workspace states.

assumptions_latex: An algorithm simultaneously retains \(r_k\) dense symmetric iterate arrays for PSD block \(k\).
Each array uses packed symmetric storage.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iterate footprint is \(M_{\mathrm{it}}=\sum_{k=1}^q r_k n_k(n_k+1)/2\) scalar locations.

notation.meaning: number of retained arrays for block k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Packed storage for simultaneously live dense symmetric block iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If an implementation simultaneously retains \(r_k\) dense symmetric arrays for PSD block \(k\), each of order \(n_k\), its packed iterate-storage footprint is \(M_{\mathrm{it}}=\sum_{k=1}^q r_k n_k(n_k+1)/2\) scalar locations. Full square storage replaces each summand by \(r_kn_k^2\). Workspace, factorization data, sparse indices, and replicated copies are excluded unless explicitly added, so the storage convention and set of live arrays form part of the reported footprint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Iterate storage sums the packed symmetric sizes of all simultaneously live block arrays; workspaces, indices, and replicas must be added separately.
knowledge_statements.title: Iterate Storage Footprint

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The accounting formula is internally correct under packed symmetric storage, but the implementation model and exclusions are unsupported by an inspectable source.

children.title: Communication Volume
children.top_down_role: Data movement imposed by distributed matrix and operator workloads.

assumptions_latex: A distributed iteration executes a specified set \(\mathcal M_t\) of point-to-point or collective messages.
Message payloads are measured in scalar words.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The per-iteration communication volume is \(V_t=\sum_{e\in\mathcal M_t}|e|\) scalar words.

notation.meaning: payload size of message e in scalar words

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Payload volume for a fixed distributed execution and counting convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For distributed iteration \(t\), let \(\mathcal M_t\) be the multiset of transmitted messages and let \(|e|\) denote the payload of message \(e\) in scalar words. The aggregate communication volume is \(V_t=\sum_{e\in\mathcal M_t}|e|\). A report must state whether collective traffic is counted once logically or as all network transmissions. Latency, synchronization delay, protocol headers, and local memory movement are distinct resources and are not included in \(V_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Communication volume is the sum of transmitted payload words per iteration under an explicit convention for counting collective operations.
knowledge_statements.title: Communication Volume

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The payload-sum convention is coherent and fits the communication-volume leaf, but no source supports the definition or the alternative collective-traffic conventions.

children.title: Synchronization Pressure
children.top_down_role: Latency and coordination limits caused by globally coupled computation.

assumptions_latex: A distributed iteration has a dependency directed acyclic graph \(D_t\).
A synchronization event blocks progress until designated participants complete preceding work.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Synchronization pressure is summarized by the number and critical-path depth of blocking collective events in \(D_t\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Blocking collective dependencies in one distributed SDP iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent iteration \(t\) by a dependency directed acyclic graph \(D_t\). Let \(B_t\) count its blocking collective events, and let \(L_t\) be the maximum number of such events on any dependency path. The pair \((B_t,L_t)\) is a synchronization-pressure profile: \(B_t\) measures frequency, while \(L_t\) measures unavoidable sequential depth. It is distinct from communication volume because even a small-message global reduction can add a blocking critical-path stage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Synchronization pressure records how many blocking collectives occur and how many lie sequentially on the iteration's critical dependency path.
knowledge_statements.title: Synchronization Pressure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pair consisting of blocking-event count and synchronization depth is a plausible profile, but it is a chosen formalization rather than a uniquely standard definition. No inspectable source supports it.

children.title: Aggregate Sparsity Pattern
children.top_down_role: Global nonzero structure induced by the combined SDP data.

assumptions_latex: The SDP data are symmetric matrices \(C,A_1,\ldots,A_m\in\mathbb S^n\).
Structural nonzeros are determined before numerical cancellation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The aggregate sparsity graph has edge \(\{u,v\}\) exactly when some data matrix has a structurally nonzero \((u,v)\) entry.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Union sparsity graph of all objective and constraint matrices.

source_refs.locator: 4.6 Exploiting Sparsity p. 91
source_refs.source_title: Moments, Positive Polynomials and Their Applications

source_refs.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given symmetric SDP data \(C,A_1,\ldots,A_m\in\mathbb S^n\), their aggregate sparsity graph is \(G_{\mathrm{agg}}=([n],E)\), where for distinct \(u,v\in[n]\), \(\{u,v\}\in E\) if and only if \(C_{uv}\) or \((A_i)_{uv}\) is structurally nonzero for some \(i\). Diagonal activity may be recorded as vertex metadata. Thus \(G_{\mathrm{agg}}\) is the union of the structural sparsity patterns of all SDP data matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The aggregate sparsity pattern is the union graph of structural nonzeros across the objective and every constraint matrix.
knowledge_statements.title: Aggregate Sparsity Pattern

children.title: Block Sparsity Pattern
children.top_down_role: Structured nonzero organization within or across matrix blocks.

assumptions_latex: The matrix indices are partitioned into nonempty blocks \([n]=I_1\dot\cup\cdots\dot\cup I_q\).
The SDP data are \(C,A_1,\ldots,A_m\in\mathbb S^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The block sparsity graph joins \(a\) and \(b\) exactly when some data submatrix on \(I_a\times I_b\) is structurally nonzero.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quotient-level sparsity induced by a fixed partition of matrix indices.

source_refs.locator: 8.1 Exploiting sparsity p. 130
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Polynomial and Semi-Algebraic Optimization

source_refs.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a partition \([n]=I_1\dot\cup\cdots\dot\cup I_q\). The block sparsity graph is \(G_{\mathrm{blk}}=([q],E_{\mathrm{blk}})\), where distinct blocks \(a,b\) satisfy \(\{a,b\}\in E_{\mathrm{blk}}\) if and only if at least one submatrix \(C[I_a,I_b]\) or \(A_i[I_a,I_b]\) contains a structural nonzero. Equivalently, it is the quotient support pattern obtained by contracting each index block in the aggregate sparsity graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Block sparsity contracts a fixed index partition and marks two blocks adjacent when any SDP data matrix couples them structurally.
knowledge_statements.title: Block Sparsity Pattern

children.title: Cross-Block Coupling
children.top_down_role: Couplings that limit independent treatment of sparse blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Block Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines coupling between prescribed matrix blocks through the aggregate support of SDP data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V_1,\ldots,V_q\) partition \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and consider SDP data \(C,A_1,\ldots,A_m\in\mathbb S^n\). The cross-block coupling graph has vertex set \(\{1,\ldots,q\}\) and an edge \(\{k,\ell\}\), with \(k
e\ell\), precisely when \(C[V_k,V_\ell]
e0\) or \(A_i[V_k,V_\ell]
e0\) for some \(i\). The blocks are uncoupled exactly when this graph has no edges; otherwise each connected component identifies a collection of blocks linked through off-diagonal problem data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two matrix blocks are coupled when an objective or constraint matrix has a nonzero off-diagonal submatrix between them.
assumptions_latex: \(V_1,\ldots,V_q\) is a partition of the matrix indices.
\(C,A_1,\ldots,A_m\in\mathbb S^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{k,\ell\}\in E\iff C[V_k,V_\ell]\ne0\ \text{or}\ \exists i:\ A_i[V_k,V_\ell]\ne0\).

notation.meaning: Submatrix of M with row indices in V_k and column indices in V_ell.
Edge set of the cross-block coupling graph.

children.title: Low-Rank Problem Data
children.top_down_role: Compact rank structure in objectives, constraints, and operator coefficients.

knowledge_statements.title: Low-Rank Problem Data
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses uniformly bounded matrix ranks as the structural signature of low-rank SDP data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an SDP with objective matrix \(C\in\mathbb S^n\) and constraint matrices \(A_i\in\mathbb S^n\), the data are rank-bounded by \(r\) when \(\operatorname{rank}(C)\le r\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(A_i)\le r\) for every \(i\). Equivalently, each datum admits a signed factorization \(A_i=U_iD_iU_i^{\mathsf T}\), and likewise for \(C\), with at most \(r\) columns in its factor matrix and a real diagonal signature matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The SDP data are rank-bounded by r when the objective matrix and every constraint matrix have rank at most r.
assumptions_latex: \(C,A_1,\ldots,A_m\in\mathbb S^n\).
\(0\le r\le n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{\operatorname{rank}(C),\operatorname{rank}(A_1),\ldots,\operatorname{rank}(A_m)\}\le r\).

notation.meaning: Uniform rank bound for the SDP data matrices.
Signed spectral factorization of a symmetric data matrix.

children.title: Low-Rank Solution Geometry
children.top_down_role: Rank profiles associated with feasible or optimal primal states.

knowledge_statements.title: Low-Rank Solution Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents rank-bounded PSD solutions through factors and faces of the semidefinite cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X\in\mathbb S_+^n\), the condition \(\operatorname{rank}(X)\le r\) holds if and only if \(X=YY^{\mathsf T}\) for some \(Y\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}\). If the range of \(X\) is contained in a fixed subspace \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) with orthonormal basis matrix \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}\), then \(X=QSQ^{\mathsf T}\) for some \(S\in\mathbb S_+^r\). The latter set is a face of \(\mathbb S_+^n\) linearly isomorphic to \(\mathbb S_+^r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Low-rank PSD matrices factor through few columns; fixing their range places them in a smaller semidefinite face.
assumptions_latex: \(X\in\mathbb S_+^n\).
\(0\le r\le n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}(X)\le r\iff \exists Y\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}:X=YY^{\mathsf T}\).

notation.meaning: Cone of real symmetric positive semidefinite n-by-n matrices.
Orthonormal basis matrix for the prescribed range subspace.

children.title: Data–Solution Rank Alignment
children.top_down_role: Regimes where input rank structure does or does not predict solution rank.

knowledge_statements.title: Data–Solution Rank Alignment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies alignment between low-dimensional data ranges and the range of an optimal PSD solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_\star\in\mathbb S_+^n\) be an optimal solution and let \(D=\operatorname{span}(\operatorname{range}(C),\operatorname{range}(A_1),\ldots,\operatorname{range}(A_m))\). Data–solution rank alignment with a subspace \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) holds when \(D\subseteq U\), \(\operatorname{range}(X_\star)\subseteq U\), and \(\dim U=r<n\). Under this condition all data matrices and the selected solution vanish on \(U^\perp\), so they admit simultaneous compression to symmetric matrices of order \(r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rank alignment holds when all data ranges and an optimal solution range lie in one proper low-dimensional subspace.
assumptions_latex: \(C,A_1,\ldots,A_m,X_\star\in\mathbb S^n\) and \(X_\star\succeq0\).
\(X_\star\) is optimal for the SDP under consideration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D+\operatorname{range}(X_\star)\subseteq U\ \text{and}\ \dim U=r<n\).

notation.meaning: Linear span of the ranges of all SDP data matrices.
Common compression subspace for data and solution.
A selected optimal positive semidefinite solution.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports this specific data–solution alignment predicate.
standard_field_rationale: simultaneous range containment is the exact linear-algebraic condition for common orthogonal compression.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The simultaneous range-containment condition is algebraically plausible, but no source is supplied for this particular data–solution alignment concept or its role as an SDP structural signature.

children.title: Group-Invariant SDP Structure
children.top_down_role: Problem components preserved under group actions.

knowledge_statements.title: Group-Invariant SDP Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines invariance of an SDP under orthogonal conjugation by a finite or compact group.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite or compact group \(G\) act orthogonally through \(\rho:G\to O(n)\). An SDP feasible set \(\mathcal F\subseteq\mathbb S_+^n\) is group-invariant when \(X\in\mathcal F\) implies \(\rho(g)X\rho(g)^{\mathsf T}\in\mathcal F\) for every \(g\in G\). The objective is invariant when \(\langle C,\rho(g)X\rho(g)^{\mathsf T}\rangle=\langle C,X\rangle\). An SDP has group-invariant structure when both conditions hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An SDP is group-invariant when conjugating a feasible matrix by any group action preserves feasibility and objective value.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite or compact.
\(\rho:G\to O(n)\) is an orthogonal representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\in\mathcal F\Rightarrow \rho(g)X\rho(g)^{\mathsf T}\in\mathcal F\) and \(\langle C,\rho(g)X\rho(g)^{\mathsf T}\rangle=\langle C,X\rangle\).

notation.meaning: Orthogonal representation of the symmetry group.

children.title: Invariant Matrix Algebras
children.top_down_role: Matrix subalgebras supporting symmetry-adapted representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Invariant Matrix Algebras
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the commutant algebra associated with an orthogonal group representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an orthogonal representation \(\rho:G\to O(n)\), the invariant matrix algebra is the commutant \(\mathcal A_G=\{M\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}:M\rho(g)=\rho(g)M\ \text{for every }g\in G\}\). It is a unital real algebra closed under transpose. Its symmetric part equals the fixed-point subspace for conjugation: \(\mathcal A_G\cap\mathbb S^n=\{X\in\mathbb S^n:\rho(g)X\rho(g)^{\mathsf T}=X\ \text{for every }g\in G\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The invariant matrix algebra consists of matrices commuting with every group-representation matrix; its symmetric part is fixed under conjugation.
assumptions_latex: \(\rho:G\to O(n)\) is an orthogonal representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A_G\cap\mathbb S^n=\operatorname{Fix}(X\mapsto\rho(g)X\rho(g)^{\mathsf T}:g\in G)\).

notation.meaning: Space of real symmetric n-by-n matrices.

children.title: Symmetry–Algebra Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Translation between group actions and algebraic block structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry–Algebra Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States Reynolds averaging and reduction of an invariant SDP to the commutant algebra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be finite or compact, with normalized Haar measure \(\mu\), and let \(\rho:G\to O(n)\). Suppose an SDP has a convex group-invariant feasible set \(\mathcal F\) and invariant linear objective \(\langle C,X\rangle\). Then the Reynolds average \(\mathcal R(X)=\int_G\rho(g)X\rho(g)^{\mathsf T}\,d\mu(g)\) belongs to \(\mathcal F\cap\mathcal A_G\), is positive semidefinite whenever \(X\) is, and has the same objective value. Consequently, if an optimum is attained, an optimal solution exists in \(\mathcal A_G\cap\mathbb S_+^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Averaging any feasible solution over the symmetry group produces an equally good feasible solution in the invariant algebra.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite or compact and \(\rho:G\to O(n)\).
\(\mathcal F\) is convex and invariant under conjugation by \(\rho(G)\).
The linear objective is invariant and its optimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists X_\star\in\mathcal F\cap\mathcal A_G\cap\mathbb S_+^n\) attaining the SDP optimum.

notation.meaning: Normalized Haar probability measure on the group.
Commutant algebra of the group representation.

children.title: Degenerate Feasible Geometry
children.top_down_role: Lower-dimensional feasibility and regularity-loss regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Feasible Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies semidefinite feasibility confined to a proper face and therefore lacking strict feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the nonempty feasible set \(\mathcal F=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\mathcal A(X)=b\}\), degenerate feasible geometry means that \(\mathcal F\cap\mathbb S_{++}^n=\varnothing\). Equivalently, the minimal face of \(\mathbb S_+^n\) containing \(\mathcal F\) is proper. Hence there is a proper subspace \(U\subsetneq\mathbb R^n\) such that every feasible matrix satisfies \(\operatorname{range}(X)\subseteq U\), or equivalently has a common nonzero kernel direction in \(U^\perp\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty SDP feasible set is geometrically degenerate when it contains no positive definite matrix and lies in a proper PSD face.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F=\{X\succeq0:\mathcal A(X)=b\}\) is nonempty.
The ambient cone is \(\mathbb S_+^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F\cap\mathbb S_{++}^n=\varnothing\iff \operatorname{face}(\mathcal F)\subsetneq\mathbb S_+^n\).

notation.meaning: Minimal face of the PSD cone containing the feasible set.
Range subspace defining that minimal face.

children.title: Exposed-Face Structure
children.top_down_role: Faces identified by supporting dual geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Exposed-Face Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents every face of the positive semidefinite cone by an exposing PSD matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Z\in\mathbb S_+^n\), the set \(F_Z=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\langle Z,X\rangle=0\}\) is an exposed face of \(\mathbb S_+^n\), and \(F_Z=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\operatorname{range}(X)\subseteq\ker Z\}\). Conversely, every face of \(\mathbb S_+^n\) has this form for some \(Z\succeq0\). Thus an orthonormal basis \(Q\) of \(\ker Z\) gives \(F_Z=\{QYQ^{\mathsf T}:Y\in\mathbb S_+^r\}\), where \(r=\dim\ker Z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every PSD-cone face is exposed by a PSD matrix and consists of matrices whose ranges lie in the exposer's kernel.
assumptions_latex: \(Z\in\mathbb S_+^n\).
\(Q\) has orthonormal columns spanning \(\ker Z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_Z=\{X\succeq0:\langle Z,X\rangle=0\}=\{QYQ^{\mathsf T}:Y\in\mathbb S_+^r\}\).

notation.meaning: Face exposed by the positive semidefinite matrix Z.
Orthonormal basis matrix for the kernel of Z.
Dimension of the kernel of Z.

children.title: Facial-Reduction Implications
children.top_down_role: Dimension, conditioning, and certificate consequences of hidden face structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Facial-Reduction Implications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduces a degenerate SDP to its minimal face using exposing certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\mathcal F=\{X\in K:\mathcal A(X)=b\}\) with \(K=\mathbb S_+^n\), initialize \(K_0=K\). At step \(j\), find \(y_j\) such that \(Z_j=\mathcal A^*y_j\in K_j^*\setminus K_j^\perp\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}y_j=0\), then set \(K_{j+1}=K_j\cap Z_j^\perp\). Every feasible matrix remains in \(K_{j+1}\). Stop when the affine constraints have a relative-interior feasible point in \(K_j\); output the reduced cone and the equivalent restricted feasibility problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Facial reduction repeatedly uses dual exposing certificates to restrict a degenerate SDP to a smaller face containing every feasible matrix.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\mathcal A(X)=b\}\) is nonempty.
Each selected certificate satisfies the displayed dual-cone and orthogonality conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F\subseteq K_{j+1}\subsetneq K_j\) until relative strict feasibility holds in the final face.

notation.meaning: Current face used as the reduced cone.
Adjoint of the linear constraint map.

children.title: Partially Separable Cone Structure
children.top_down_role: Cone organization admitting overlapping local components.

knowledge_statements.title: Partially Separable Cone Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a cone through lower-dimensional conic restrictions on overlapping coordinate subsets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E_k:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^{n_k}\) be coordinate-selection maps and let \(K_k\subseteq\mathbb R^{n_k}\) be closed convex cones. The cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is partially separable with respect to these maps when \(K=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:E_kx\in K_k\ \text{for all }k=1,\ldots,q\}\). Unlike a direct product, the selected coordinate sets may overlap; variables appearing in multiple selections provide the coupling between otherwise local conic conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partially separable cone is defined by lower-dimensional conic constraints on possibly overlapping groups of coordinates.
assumptions_latex: \(E_k\) are fixed coordinate-selection maps.
Each \(K_k\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in K\iff E_kx\in K_k\ \text{for every }k\).

notation.meaning: Selection map for the k-th coordinate group.
Local cone associated with the k-th group.

children.title: Coupling Interfaces

knowledge_statements.title: Coupling Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents partial separability using local variable copies joined by linear consistency constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E:x\mapsto(E_1x,\ldots,E_qx)\) collect the local selections and choose a linear map \(B\) satisfying \(\ker B=\operatorname{range}E\). Then membership in the partially separable cone has the lifted representation \(x\in K\) if and only if there are local variables \(y_k\in K_k\) such that \(y=(y_1,\ldots,y_q)=Ex\); equivalently, the local variables satisfy \(y_k\in K_k\) and the interface equations \(By=0\). For coordinate selections, these equations enforce equality of copies on every shared coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local conic variables can be coupled exactly by linear equations that equate their copies on overlapping coordinates.
assumptions_latex: \(K=\{x:E_kx\in K_k\text{ for all }k\}\).
\(E\) is injective on the modeled global variable space.
\(B\) is chosen so that \(\ker B=\operatorname{range}E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E(K)=\{y:y_k\in K_k\ \forall k,\ By=0\}\).

notation.meaning: Local copy of the variables selected by E_k.

children.title: Separability Breakdown
children.top_down_role: Dense or global interactions that defeat useful decomposition.

knowledge_statements.title: Separability Breakdown
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of blockwise decomposition relative to a fixed partition of SDP variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\ge 2\), let \(n_1,\ldots,n_p\) be positive integers, and write \(X=(X_1,\ldots,X_p)\) with \(X_j\in\mathbb S^{n_j}\). Let \(F\subseteq\prod_{j=1}^p\mathbb S^{n_j}\) be nonempty and let \(f:F\to\mathbb R\). Relative to proposed nonempty local sets \(F_j\subseteq\mathbb S^{n_j}\) and functions \(f_j:F_j\to\mathbb R\), exact separability means \(F=\prod_{j=1}^pF_j\) and \(f(X)=\sum_{j=1}^p f_j(X_j)\) for every \(X\in F\). If either condition fails, this proposed independent block decomposition is not exact, and independently minimizing the local functions is not guaranteed to produce a feasible or optimal point of the original problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proposed block decomposition is not exact if its feasible set is not Cartesian or its objective is not additive; independent local minimization then has no general feasibility or optimality guarantee.
assumptions_latex: \(p\ge 2\) and \(n_j\ge 1\) for \(j=1,\ldots,p\).
\(F\) and every proposed local feasible set \(F_j\) are nonempty.
The decomposition is assessed relative to the fixed block partition and proposed local components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(F\ne\prod_{j=1}^pF_j\) or if \(f(X)\ne\sum_{j=1}^pf_j(X_j)\) for some \(X\in F\), exact independent decomposition with these local components fails.

notation.meaning: proposed local feasible set for block j
proposed local objective contribution for block j

children.title: Forward Operator Access
children.top_down_role: Availability, cost, and workspace characteristics of forward operator actions.

knowledge_statements.title: Forward Operator Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matrix-free evaluation of the primal SDP constraint operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For coefficient matrices \(A_1,\ldots,A_m\in\mathbb S^n\), the forward linear operator is \(\mathcal A:\mathbb S^n\to\mathbb R^m\) defined by \([\mathcal A(X)]_i=\langle A_i,X\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(A_iX)\). Forward operator access is an oracle that, for every supplied \(X\in\mathbb S^n\), returns this vector without requiring the caller to materialize the matrices \(A_i\). The implementation may use explicit sparse data, factored coefficients, transforms, or generated actions, provided the returned mapping is linear and has the displayed values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A forward oracle returns all coefficient inner products with a symmetric input matrix, without requiring explicit coefficient matrices.
assumptions_latex: \(A_i\in\mathbb S^n\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
The matrix inner product is \(\langle U,V\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(UV)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A(X)=(\langle A_1,X\rangle,\ldots,\langle A_m,X\rangle)\).

children.title: Adjoint Operator Access
children.top_down_role: Availability, cost, and workspace characteristics of adjoint operator actions.

knowledge_statements.title: Adjoint Operator Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matrix-free evaluation of the dual SDP constraint operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the forward map \([\mathcal A(X)]_i=\langle A_i,X\rangle\), its adjoint is \(\mathcal A^*:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb S^n\) given by \(\mathcal A^*(y)=\sum_{i=1}^m y_iA_i\). Adjoint operator access is an oracle that returns this symmetric matrix, or an equivalent structured representation accepted by subsequent computations, without requiring the caller to assemble every coefficient matrix separately. Its defining property is \(\langle\mathcal A(X),y\rangle_{\mathbb R^m}=\langle X,\mathcal A^*(y)\rangle\) for all admissible \(X\) and \(y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adjoint oracle accumulates a weighted sum of coefficient matrices and satisfies the defining inner-product identity with the forward map.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A:\mathbb S^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear.
Both spaces carry their standard Euclidean inner products.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A^*(y)=\sum_{i=1}^m y_iA_i\) and \(\langle\mathcal A(X),y\rangle=\langle X,\mathcal A^*(y)\rangle\).

children.title: Operator-Pair Consistency
children.top_down_role: Compatibility and numerical agreement between paired operator interfaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Operator-Pair Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact and numerical compatibility condition for a forward-adjoint oracle pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A linear oracle pair \((\widehat{\mathcal A},\widehat{\mathcal A}^*)\), with \(\widehat{\mathcal A}:\mathbb S^n\to\mathbb R^m\) and \(\widehat{\mathcal A}^*:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb S^n\), is exactly consistent when \(\langle\widehat{\mathcal A}(X),y\rangle_{\mathbb R^m}=\langle X,\widehat{\mathcal A}^*(y)\rangle_F\) for every \(X\in\mathbb S^n\) and \(y\in\mathbb R^m\). Given \(\tau\ge0\) and a test set \(T\subseteq\mathbb S^n\times\mathbb R^m\), the pair is empirically consistent on \(T\) at tolerance \(\tau\) when \(\left|\langle\widehat{\mathcal A}(X),y\rangle_{\mathbb R^m}-\langle X,\widehat{\mathcal A}^*(y)\rangle_F\right|\le\tau\|X\|_F\|y\|_2\) for every \((X,y)\in T\). A violated test reveals inconsistency, whereas passing a proper subset \(T\) does not establish exact consistency on the full product space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forward and adjoint routines are exactly consistent when their bilinear inner products agree for every input pair; a finite tolerance test establishes only consistency on the tested pairs.
assumptions_latex: \(\widehat{\mathcal A}:\mathbb S^n\to\mathbb R^m\) and \(\widehat{\mathcal A}^*:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb S^n\) are linear.
\(T\subseteq\mathbb S^n\times\mathbb R^m\) and \(\tau\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Empirical consistency on \(T\) means \(\left|\langle\widehat{\mathcal A}(X),y\rangle_{\mathbb R^m}-\langle X,\widehat{\mathcal A}^*(y)\rangle_F\right|\le\tau\|X\|_F\|y\|_2\) for every \((X,y)\in T\).

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Sparse Coefficient Storage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sparse materialization model for SDP coefficient matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(A_1,\ldots,A_m\in\mathbb S^n\), explicit sparse coefficient storage records the index-value triples of one triangle of each \(A_i\), together with matrix boundaries and dimensions. The omitted triangle is determined by symmetry. If \(s=\sum_{i=1}^m\operatorname{nnz}_{\triangle}(A_i)\), storage is \(O(s+m+n)\) machine words, excluding solver outputs. Forward products are sparse inner products, and adjoint products accumulate \(y_iA_i\) over stored entries while applying the chosen off-diagonal symmetry convention exactly once.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each symmetric coefficient matrix is stored by sparse triangular entries, enabling sparse forward inner products and adjoint accumulation.
assumptions_latex: \(A_i\in\mathbb S^n\) have explicitly enumerable nonzero entries.
A fixed triangular and off-diagonal weighting convention is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coefficient representation requires \(O(s+m+n)\) words for \(s=\sum_i\operatorname{nnz}_{\triangle}(A_i)\).

notation.meaning: number of stored entries in the selected triangle

knowledge_statements.title: Implicit Structured Coefficient Actions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operator representation that avoids materializing structured SDP coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An implicit structured coefficient model represents \(A_1,\ldots,A_m\in\mathbb S^n\) by routines evaluating \(X\mapsto(\langle A_i,X\rangle)_{i=1}^m\) and \(y\mapsto\sum_{i=1}^m y_iA_i\), rather than by stored matrix entries. Parameters may encode low-rank factors, Kronecker products, convolutional transforms, or generated blocks. The representation is valid only when both routines implement linear maps and satisfy \(\langle\mathcal A(X),y\rangle=\langle X,\mathcal A^*(y)\rangle\) under the same inner-product and symmetry conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Structured parameters and routines replace explicit coefficients while preserving the exact forward map, adjoint map, and inner-product identity.
assumptions_latex: The structured parameters determine fixed linear coefficient actions.
Forward and adjoint routines use identical scaling and symmetry conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The routines realize \(\mathcal A(X)=(\langle A_i,X\rangle)_i\) and \(\mathcal A^*(y)=\sum_i y_iA_i\) without explicit coefficient storage.

knowledge_statements.title: Streaming Workspace
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded-memory evaluation by sequential batches of coefficient data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a partition \(I_1,\ldots,I_B\) of \(\{1,\ldots,m\}\), an input \(X\) or \(y\), and a batch loader. For a forward call, initialize \(z\in\mathbb R^m\); load batch \(I_b\), set \(z_i=\langle A_i,X\rangle\) for \(i\in I_b\), and release the batch. For an adjoint call, initialize \(S=0\); load \(I_b\), update \(S\leftarrow S+\sum_{i\in I_b}y_iA_i\), and release the batch. Stop after \(B\) batches and output \(z\) or \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coefficient batches are loaded, applied, and released sequentially, bounding resident coefficient memory by the largest batch.
assumptions_latex: The batches form a disjoint cover of all coefficient indices.
Each loaded batch reproduces its coefficients exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Peak coefficient workspace is \(O(\max_b s_b)\), apart from the input, output, and accumulator.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Operator Workspace
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Data-parallel evaluation of SDP forward and adjoint operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition \(\{1,\ldots,m\}=I_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}I_P\) and place coefficients indexed by \(I_p\) on worker \(p\). For a forward call, broadcast or distribute \(X\); worker \(p\) computes \(z_i=\langle A_i,X\rangle\) for \(i\in I_p\), and the disjoint subvectors are concatenated. For an adjoint call, worker \(p\) forms \(S_p=\sum_{i\in I_p}y_iA_i\); a sum reduction returns \(S=\sum_{p=1}^P S_p=\mathcal A^*(y)\). Output follows after the required collective communication completes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Workers own disjoint coefficient subsets; forward results concatenate, while adjoint partial matrices are summed by a collective reduction.
assumptions_latex: Every coefficient index belongs to exactly one worker subset.
All workers use compatible matrix layouts and arithmetic conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The distributed calls return \(z=\mathcal A(X)\) and \(S=\mathcal A^*(y)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Expensive Adjoint Accumulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: When matrix-free coefficient access does not make the adjoint inexpensive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\mathcal A^*(y)=\sum_{i=1}^m y_iA_i\in\mathbb S^n\). If an algorithm requires this output as an explicit dense matrix and there exists an admissible \(y\) for which \(\mathcal A^*(y)\) has \(\Theta(n^2)\) independently representable entries, then any explicit adjoint evaluation requires \(\Omega(n^2)\) output storage and writes. Consequently, implicit or sparse storage of the individual \(A_i\) alone cannot yield a subquadratic explicit-adjoint workspace bound; avoiding the boundary requires a structured output representation or downstream matrix-free consumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adjoint with a generically dense explicit output necessarily incurs quadratic storage and write cost despite implicit coefficients.
assumptions_latex: The computational interface requires an explicit dense representation of \(\mathcal A^*(y)\).
Some admissible output has \(\Theta(n^2)\) independent entries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Explicit adjoint accumulation has storage and write complexity \(\Omega(n^2)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Hidden Dense Intermediates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Peak-memory failure caused by dense internal materialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an operator implementation accepts a sparse or implicit input representation of size \(s=o(n^2)\), but during evaluation materializes an unrestricted matrix \(D\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\). If \(D\) is live before the routine releases its other required data, then peak workspace is at least \(\Omega(n^2)\) machine words, regardless of the external coefficient-storage bound. Thus an advertised matrix-free or sparse interface does not imply subquadratic memory unless every simultaneously live intermediate also admits a subquadratic representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dense internal matrix forces quadratic peak memory even when inputs and public operator interfaces are sparse or implicit.
assumptions_latex: The intermediate \(D\) is explicitly stored as an unrestricted dense matrix.
Machine words store only a constant number of matrix entries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Materializing \(D\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) forces peak workspace \(\Omega(n^2)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Operator Recomputation Overhead
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Time overhead from repeatedly regenerating unchanged operator data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an iterative SDP method make \(N\) operator calls. Suppose each call regenerates unchanged structured data at cost \(C_{\mathrm{gen}}>0\) and then applies the operator at cost \(C_{\mathrm{app}}\). Without caching, total work is at least \(N(C_{\mathrm{gen}}+C_{\mathrm{app}})\); if the generated data can be cached once, the corresponding bound is \(C_{\mathrm{gen}}+NC_{\mathrm{app}}\). Recomputation is asymptotically dominant when \(C_{\mathrm{gen}}/C_{\mathrm{app}}\to\infty\), and it negates cheap matrix-free actions unless storage limits or changing parameters make caching unavailable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly regenerating invariant operator data adds linear-in-iterations overhead and may dominate the actual structured action.
assumptions_latex: The generated operator data are invariant across the \(N\) calls.
Generation and application costs are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Avoidable recomputation overhead equals \((N-1)C_{\mathrm{gen}}\) relative to one-time caching.

knowledge_statements.title: Chordal Graph Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite undirected chordality used in sparse semidefinite decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) is chordal when every simple cycle \((v_1,\ldots,v_k,v_1)\) of length \(k\ge4\) contains a chord: there exist nonconsecutive cycle vertices \(v_i\) and \(v_j\) such that \(\{v_i,v_j\}\in E\). Equivalently, \(G\) has no induced cycle of length at least four. In sparse semidefinite optimization, this definition is applied to the aggregate sparsity graph whose vertices index matrix rows and columns and whose edges mark permitted off-diagonal entries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph is chordal exactly when every cycle of length at least four has an edge joining two nonconsecutive cycle vertices.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite, simple, and undirected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) is chordal if and only if it has no induced cycle of length \(k\ge4\).

knowledge_statements.title: Perfect-Elimination Orderings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite undirected graphs; the ordering convention eliminates lower-indexed vertices first.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph and let \(\pi=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\) order \(V\). For each \(i\), define the later-neighbor set \(N_i^+=\{v_j:j>i,\ \{v_i,v_j\}\in E\}\). The ordering \(\pi\) is a perfect-elimination ordering if \(N_i^+\) is a clique of \(G\) for every \(i\); equivalently, eliminating vertices in the order \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) introduces no fill edges. A finite graph is chordal if and only if it admits a perfect-elimination ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ordering is perfect when every vertex's later neighbors form a clique; exactly the chordal graphs admit such an ordering.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite, simple, and undirected.
\(\pi\) is a bijective ordering of \(V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi\text{ is perfect}\iff \forall i,\ G[N_i^+]\text{ is complete}\), and \(G\text{ is chordal}\iff G\text{ has such a }\pi\).

notation.meaning: Neighbors of the ith vertex occurring later in the ordering.

children.title: Minimal Separators

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal Separators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertex separators in finite undirected graphs, with the separated vertices made explicit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph and let \(a,b\in V\) be distinct and nonadjacent. A set \(S\subseteq V\setminus\{a,b\}\) is an \(a\)-\(b\) separator if \(a\) and \(b\) lie in different connected components of \(G-S\). It is a minimal \(a\)-\(b\) separator if no proper subset of \(S\) is an \(a\)-\(b\) separator. A set is a minimal separator of \(G\) if it is a minimal \(a\)-\(b\) separator for some pair \(a,b\). In a chordal graph, every minimal separator induces a clique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimal separator disconnects some nonadjacent vertices, while none of its proper subsets does; in chordal graphs every such separator is a clique.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite, simple, and undirected.
\(a\ne b\) and \(\{a,b\}\notin E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\text{ is minimal}\iff S\text{ separates }a,b\text{ and no }S'\subsetneq S\text{ does};\quad G\text{ chordal}\Rightarrow G[S]\text{ complete}.

notation.meaning: Graph obtained by deleting vertices in S and their incident edges.

children.title: Maximal Cliques

knowledge_statements.title: Maximal Cliques
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inclusion-maximal cliques, as used for chordal decomposition rather than maximum-cardinality cliques.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), a set \(C\subseteq V\) is a clique if every two distinct vertices in \(C\) are adjacent. It is a maximal clique if there is no clique \(D\) satisfying \(C\subsetneq D\subseteq V\). Thus maximality is with respect to set inclusion and does not require \(C\) to have maximum cardinality. For a chordal graph equipped with a perfect-elimination ordering, every maximal clique equals \(\{v_i\}\cup N_i^+\) for some \(i\), after discarding sets properly contained in another such set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximal clique is an inclusion-maximal complete vertex set; under perfect elimination, maximal later-neighbor cliques generate all maximal cliques.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite, simple, and undirected.
For the ordering characterization, \(G\) is chordal and \((v_1,\ldots,v_n)\) is perfect.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ maximal}\iff C\text{ is a clique and }\nexists D\text{ clique with }C\subsetneq D\);\quad \mathcal C_{\max}=\max_{\subseteq}\{\{v_i\}\cup N_i^+\}_{i=1}^n.\)

notation.meaning: Family of maximal cliques of G.
Later neighbors of the ith vertex.

knowledge_statements.title: Separator–Clique Incidence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clique-tree incidence representation of separators in a connected chordal graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a connected chordal graph, let \(\mathcal C\) be its maximal cliques, and let \(T=(\mathcal C,F)\) be a clique tree satisfying the running-intersection property. Label each tree edge \(e=\{C,D\}\) by \(S_e=C\cap D\). Then \(S_e\) is a minimal separator of \(G\). Conversely, every minimal separator \(S\) occurs as \(S=C\cap D\) on at least one edge of every clique tree. Hence the edge-to-separator incidence relation \(e\mapsto S_e\) may be many-to-one, while each incident clique contains its edge label.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clique-tree edges are labeled by intersections of adjacent maximal cliques; these labels are precisely the graph's minimal separators, possibly with repetitions.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite, connected, and chordal.
\(T\) is a clique tree on all maximal cliques of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{S_e:e\in F\}=\{S:S\text{ is a minimal separator of }G\}\), with equality understood after removing repeated labels.

notation.meaning: Intersection labeling the clique-tree edge e.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical edge-intersection representation of minimal separators in clique trees

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the separator-clique incidence leaf, but the claim that the edge labels of every clique tree are exactly all minimal separators is a nontrivial theorem requiring a chordal-graph source with a precise theorem, section, or page locator.

children.title: Elimination Trees

knowledge_statements.title: Elimination Trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elimination tree of an ordered chordal completion, oriented from each vertex toward its parent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=(V,F)\) be a chordal graph with perfect-elimination ordering \((v_1,\ldots,v_n)\). For each \(i\) having a later neighbor, define \(p(v_i)=v_j\), where \(j=\min\{k>i:\{v_i,v_k\}\in F\}\). Join \(v_i\) to \(p(v_i)\). Vertices without later neighbors are roots. The resulting directed graph is the elimination forest; it is an elimination tree when \(H\) is connected. Along every parent arc the ordering index strictly increases, so cycles are impossible, and each nonroot vertex has exactly one parent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each vertex is parented by its earliest later neighbor in the filled chordal graph, producing an elimination forest and, when connected, a tree.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is finite and chordal.
\((v_1,\ldots,v_n)\) is a perfect-elimination ordering.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(v_i)=v_{\min\{k>i:\{v_i,v_k\}\in F\}}\); the parent arcs form a rooted forest, and a rooted tree if \(H\) is connected.

notation.meaning: Parent of vertex vi in the elimination forest.
Ordered chordal graph, often the filled sparsity graph.

notation.meaning: Tree obtained by contracting every supernode.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quotient tree obtained by grouping structurally compatible consecutive vertices of an elimination tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be an elimination tree for an ordered filled graph. A supernode partition \(\mathcal S\) consists of disjoint, order-consecutive vertex sets whose union is \(V\), with vertices in each set sharing the prescribed identical elimination structure below their diagonal positions. Contract every set \(S\in\mathcal S\) to one node and retain an arc \(S\to R\) when an elimination-tree arc joins a vertex of \(S\) to a vertex of \(R\ne S\). When every nonroot supernode has a unique external parent supernode, the contracted graph is the supernodal tree; its separator is the common higher-index adjacency pattern used to assemble its frontal contribution into its parent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Contracting compatible consecutive elimination-tree vertices into supernodes yields a tree whose arcs describe assembly of child frontal contributions into parents.

children.title: Elimination–Supernode Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Mapping from scalar elimination dependencies to supernodal organization.

knowledge_statements.title: Elimination–Supernode Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quotient correspondence between vertex elimination and block elimination under a valid supernode partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T=(V,A)\) be an elimination tree and let \(q:V\to\mathcal S\) map each vertex to its supernode in a valid partition. For distinct supernodes \(S,R\), place the supernodal arc \(S\to R\) exactly when some \((u,p(u))\in A\) satisfies \(q(u)=S\) and \(q(p(u))=R\). Internal arcs with \(q(u)=q(p(u))\) are contracted. If each nonroot supernode has a unique external parent, this construction gives the quotient tree \(T/\mathcal S\). Thus vertexwise elimination dependencies descend to blockwise dependencies, while expanding each supernode restores the corresponding contracted portions of \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The supernodal tree is the elimination tree quotient: internal parent arcs are contracted and external parent arcs become block dependencies.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a rooted elimination tree.
\(\mathcal S\) is a valid supernode partition with unique external parents.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_{\mathcal S}=\{(q(u),q(p(u))):(u,p(u))\in A,\ q(u)\ne q(p(u))\}\), and \((\mathcal S,A_{\mathcal S})=T/\mathcal S\).

notation.meaning: Map sending a vertex to its supernode.
Arc set of the supernodal quotient tree.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quotient-map representation fits the correspondence leaf and is internally coherent once a valid supernode partition is fixed. Because validity and unique external-parent conditions depend on the selected supernode convention, a precise numerical linear algebra source is required.

children.title: Clique Trees

knowledge_statements.title: Clique Trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tree representation using all maximal cliques of a connected chordal graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a connected chordal graph and let \(\mathcal C\) be its family of maximal cliques. A clique tree is a tree \(T=(\mathcal C,F)\) such that, for every vertex \(v\in V\), the node set \(\mathcal C(v)=\{C\in\mathcal C:v\in C\}\) induces a connected subtree of \(T\). Equivalently, for any \(C,D\in\mathcal C\), every clique on the unique \(C\)-to-\(D\) path contains \(C\cap D\). Every connected chordal graph has a clique tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A clique tree connects maximal cliques so that all cliques containing any fixed graph vertex form a connected subtree.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite, connected, and chordal.
\(\mathcal C\) contains every maximal clique of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\text{ is a clique tree}\iff \forall v\in V,\ T[\mathcal C(v)]\text{ is connected}\); such a \(T\) exists.

notation.meaning: Subtree induced by cliques containing v.

children.title: Junction Trees

knowledge_statements.title: Junction Trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Running-intersection trees for general clusters, including but not limited to maximal graph cliques.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite and let \(\mathcal K\) be a finite family of subsets of \(V\), called clusters. A junction tree for \(\mathcal K\) is a tree \(T=(\mathcal K,F)\) satisfying the running-intersection condition: for every \(x\in V\), the clusters containing \(x\) induce a connected subtree. Each edge \(\{K,L\}\in F\) carries the separator label \(K\cap L\). Equivalently, whenever cluster \(M\) lies on the unique path between \(K\) and \(L\), one has \(K\cap L\subseteq M\). A clique tree is the special case in which \(\mathcal K\) is the family of maximal cliques of a chordal graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A junction tree organizes clusters so those containing any fixed variable stay connected; clique trees are its maximal-clique special case.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) and \(\mathcal K\) are finite.
The tree has exactly one node for each cluster occurrence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\text{ is a junction tree}\iff \forall x\in V,\ T[\{K\in\mathcal K:x\in K\}]\text{ is connected}.

notation.meaning: Separator label on the edge joining clusters K and L.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The general cluster-based definition and its relation to clique trees fit the junction-tree leaf and are stated consistently. No graphical-models or chordal-graph source with a specific locator is supplied.

assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a finite tree.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility predicate for a tree-indexed family of overlapping local variable sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T=(I,F)\) be a tree and let \((K_i)_{i\in I}\) be subsets of a common finite set \(V\). The family is running-intersection compatible with \(T\) if, for every \(i,j\in I\) and every node \(k\) on the unique path from \(i\) to \(j\), \(K_i\cap K_j\subseteq K_k\). Equivalently, for every \(x\in V\), the index set \(I_x=\{i\in I:x\in K_i\}\) is empty or induces a connected subtree of \(T\). This condition makes copies of any shared coordinate occur along one connected tree region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Overlapping sets are compatible when each shared element appears throughout the path between any two sets containing it.
knowledge_statements.title: Running-Intersection Compatibility
Aggregate Sparsity Graph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Entrywise aggregate sparsity of the symmetric coefficient matrices defining an SDP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider symmetric matrices \(A_0,A_1,\ldots,A_m\in\mathbb S^n\) in the affine pencil \(A(y)=A_0+\sum_{k=1}^m y_kA_k\). Its aggregate sparsity graph is \(G_{\mathrm{agg}}=(\{1,\ldots,n\},E_{\mathrm{agg}})\), where distinct vertices \(i,j\) are adjacent exactly when \((A_k)_{ij}\ne0\) for at least one \(k\in\{0,\ldots,m\}\). Diagonal positions are represented by vertices and need no loops. Thus the graph records the union of the off-diagonal sparsity patterns of all matrices participating in the semidefinite constraint, independently of the value of \(y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The aggregate sparsity graph joins indices appearing together in any nonzero off-diagonal entry of an SDP coefficient matrix.
assumptions_latex: \(A_k\in\mathbb S^n\) for \(k=0,\ldots,m\).
Structural nonzeros are determined from the supplied coefficient matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E_{\mathrm{agg}}=\{\{i,j\}:1\le i<j\le n,\ \exists k\in\{0,\ldots,m\},\ (A_k)_{ij}\ne0\}.

notation.meaning: Aggregate sparsity graph of the affine pencil.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The union-of-off-diagonal-patterns definition is precise and fits the aggregate sparsity graph leaf. No sparse-SDP source with a specific section or page locator is cited, so the convention cannot yet be source-validated.

knowledge_statements.title: Block–Hypergraph Translation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes matrix-wise block incidence from the clique-expanded correlative sparsity superpattern.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}V_p\) be the scalar-index partition and let \(A_1,\ldots,A_m\) be symmetric block matrices. Define \(\operatorname{bsupp}(A_k)=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,p\}:\exists j\text{ such that }A_k[V_i,V_j]\neq0\}\) and take \(e_k=\operatorname{bsupp}(A_k)\) as a hyperedge. The two-section has \(E_{\mathcal H}=\{\{i,j\}:i\neq j,\ \exists k,\ \{i,j\}\subseteq e_k\}\). Its clique-expanded scalar superpattern is \(E^{\mathrm{sc}}=\{\{u,v\}:u\in V_i,\ v\in V_j,\ i=j\text{ or }\{i,j\}\in E_{\mathcal H}\}\). This construction preserves matrix-wise block co-occurrence but generally does not recover the exact nonzero block pairs or scalar entries of the matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each matrix yields a hyperedge containing its incident blocks. The two-section and scalar expansion give a clique-expanded correlative sparsity superpattern, not generally the exact matrix sparsity pattern.
assumptions_latex: The scalar index set is partitioned as \(V_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}V_p\).

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Degree Ordering Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact minimum-degree elimination with arbitrary tie breaking.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(G_1=G\), \(F=\varnothing\), and an empty ordering \(\pi\). For \(k=1,\ldots,|V|\), choose a vertex \(v_k\) of minimum degree in \(G_k\), breaking ties arbitrarily. Add to \(F\) every missing edge between two vertices of \(N_{G_k}(v_k)\), thereby making that neighborhood a clique, and let \(G_{k+1}\) be the resulting graph with \(v_k\) deleted. Output \(\pi=(v_1,\ldots,v_{|V|})\) and the chordal extension \(G^+=(V,E\cup F)\). Approximate-minimum-degree variants replace the exact degree comparison by an efficiently maintained estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly eliminate a current minimum-degree vertex after completing its neighbors into a clique; the resulting fill edges form a chordal extension.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive separator ordering for chordal extension construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a recursive subproblem induced by \(W\subseteq V\), choose a separator \(S\subseteq W\) such that the components of \(G[W\setminus S]\) have vertex sets \(V_1,\ldots,V_q\). Recursively order each \(G[V_i]\), concatenate those component orderings in any order, and place the vertices of \(S\) last. Stop at singleton or prescribed small subproblems. Apply symbolic elimination to the resulting ordering \(\pi\): when a vertex is eliminated, complete its remaining neighbors into a clique. The union of the added edges with \(E\) is the output chordal extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nested dissection recursively orders separated components before their separator, then uses symbolic elimination to obtain the chordal extension.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A collection \(\mathcal Q\subseteq\mathcal B\) is structurally admissible for one clique merge when the nodes representing \(\mathcal Q\) induce a connected subtree of \(T\). Replace them by \(U=\bigcup_{B\in\mathcal Q}B\), contract that subtree to one node, and retain every edge from the subtree to an unmerged bag. Then every original bag is contained in an aggregated bag, and for each vertex \(i\), the aggregated bags containing \(i\) form a connected subtree. Thus PSD constraints on the aggregated bags provide a valid, possibly less decomposed, chordal formulation. Size or cost thresholds may select among these admissible merges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cliques may be merged by contracting connected subtrees of a clique tree; this preserves coverage and the running-intersection property.

knowledge_statements.title: Fill Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar symbolic-elimination bounds for a fixed ordering and an explicit filled-graph representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the fill count by \(f=|E^+\setminus E|=|E^+|-|E|\), and let \(d_i=|\{v_j:j>i,\ \{v_i,v_j\}\in E^+\}|\). Because every filled edge is counted once from its earlier endpoint, \(|E^+|=\sum_{i=1}^n d_i\). A standard explicit adjacency or symbolic-factor representation therefore uses \(\Theta(n+|E^+|)=\Theta(n+|E|+f)\) entries. Under the usual column-oriented scalar Cholesky model, storage is \(\Theta(\sum_{i=1}^n(d_i+1))\) and arithmetic work is \(O(\sum_{i=1}^n(d_i+1)^2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fill is the number of added edges; explicit symbolic storage is linear in the filled graph size, while squared filled-column lengths give the conventional scalar factorization-work bound.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A chordal graph on \(n\) vertices has \(m\leq n\) distinct maximal cliques. knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(i\), the later-neighbor set \(N_i^+\) is a clique in \(G^+\), and define \(d_i=|N_i^+|\). Then \(w=\max_i d_i\), so the largest clique order is \(w+1\). Every edge of \(E^+\) is counted exactly once among the later-neighbor sets, giving \(|E^+|=\sum_i d_i\) and \(f=\sum_i d_i-|E|\). The distinct maximal cliques are precisely the inclusion-maximal members among \(\{v_i\}\cup N_i^+\). Thus width is a maximum, fill is a sum, and clique complexity depends on the full distribution of the \(d_i\), not only their maximum.

knowledge_statements.title: Partially Separable Matrix Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Chordal clique representation of mutually dual partially separable matrix cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a chordal sparsity graph with maximal cliques \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\), the PSD-completable cone is partially separable:
\[
\mathcal C_E=\{X_E\in\mathbb S_E^n:R_kX_ER_k^{\mathsf T}\succeq0\text{ for }k=1,\ldots,m\}.
\]
Its dual sparse PSD cone has the additive representation
\[
\mathcal K_E=\left\{\sum_{k=1}^mR_k^{\mathsf T}Z_kR_k:Z_k\in\mathbb S_+^{|C_k|}\right\}.
\]
The first representation separates membership across clique projections; the second assembles a sparse matrix from PSD components supported on those cliques.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For chordal sparsity, completion is characterized by clique-wise PSD constraints, and sparse PSD matrices are sums of PSD matrices embedded on maximal cliques.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X_E\) be a real symmetric partial matrix whose specified positions are the edges and loops of a chordal graph \(G=(V,E)\). If \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\) are the maximal cliques of \(G\), then
\[
X_E\in P_E(\mathbb S_+^n)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad X_E[C_k,C_k]\succeq0\text{ for every }k=1,\ldots,m.
\]
Because each clique contains only specified positions, every displayed principal submatrix is fully determined. The equivalence includes singular clique matrices and therefore concerns positive-semidefinite, rather than necessarily positive-definite, completion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partial matrix on a chordal graph admits a PSD completion exactly when every fully specified maximal-clique submatrix is PSD.

\[
\exists X\in\mathbb S_{++}^n\text{ with }P_E(X)=X_E

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a chordal partial matrix \(X_E\) with positive-definite clique blocks, let \(\widehat X\) maximize \(\log\det X\) over all positive-definite completions. For any rooted clique tree with separators \(S_k=C_k\cap C_{p(k)}\),
\[
\det\widehat X=\frac{\prod_{k=1}^m\det X_E[C_k,C_k]}{\prod_{k=2}^m\det X_E[S_k,S_k]}.
\]
Consequently the completion barrier is
\[
F(X_E)=-\sum_{k=1}^m\log\det X_E[C_k,C_k]+\sum_{k=2}^m\log\det X_E[S_k,S_k].
\]
Repeated separators occur with their clique-tree multiplicities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The log-determinant barrier of a chordal completion cone equals the sum of clique barriers minus the corresponding separator barriers.
knowledge_statements.title: Completion-Barrier Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X_E\) be a partial symmetric matrix possessing a positive-definite completion. The strictly concave problem
\[
\max\{\log\det X:X\succ0,\ P_E(X)=X_E\}
\]
has a unique optimizer \(\widehat X\). It is characterized by
\[
(\widehat X^{-1})_{ij}=0\qquad\text{for every unspecified off-diagonal pair }(i,j)\notin E.
\]
Conversely, any feasible positive-definite completion satisfying these inverse-zero equations is the unique maximum-determinant completion. The inverse sparsity follows with respect to the original specified pattern, independently of whether that pattern is chordal.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected graph with maximal cliques \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\), and let \(R_k\) select the coordinates in \(C_k\). The following are equivalent: \(G\) is chordal; and every \(X\in\mathbb S_+^n\cap\mathbb S_E^n\) admits PSD matrices \(Z_k\in\mathbb S_+^{|C_k|}\) such that
\[
X=\sum_{k=1}^mR_k^{\mathsf T}Z_kR_k.
\]
Thus chordality is precisely the graph condition under which sparse positive semidefiniteness universally decomposes into positive semidefinite contributions supported on maximal cliques.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph is chordal exactly when every PSD matrix with that sparsity decomposes into PSD components supported on its maximal cliques.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a chordal graph \(G=(V,E)\), define \(\mathcal K_E=\mathbb S_+^n\cap\mathbb S_E^n\). If \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\) are its maximal cliques and \(R_k\) is the corresponding selector, then
\[
\mathcal K_E=\sum_{k=1}^mR_k^{\mathsf T}\mathbb S_+^{|C_k|}R_k
=\left\{\sum_{k=1}^mR_k^{\mathsf T}Z_kR_k:Z_k\succeq0\right\}.
\]
The summands may overlap on clique separators and need not be unique. Every assembled sum is PSD and has zeros outside \(E\), while chordality guarantees the reverse inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sparse PSD cone of a chordal graph is the Minkowski sum of PSD cones embedded on its maximal cliques.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For maximal cliques \(C_k\) of a chordal graph, define
\[
\mathcal C_E=\bigcap_{k=1}^m\{X_E:R_kX_ER_k^{\mathsf T}\succeq0\}.
\]
Under the sparse trace pairing, conic duality converts this intersection of inverse images into the clique-supported sum
\[
\mathcal C_E^*=\sum_{k=1}^mR_k^{\mathsf T}\mathbb S_+^{|C_k|}R_k=\mathcal K_E.
\]
Conversely, \(\mathcal K_E^*=\mathcal C_E\). Therefore the chordal PSD-completion criterion and the sparse clique-decomposition theorem are dual descriptions of the same pair of closed cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The chordal clique conditions for PSD completion are dual to expressing sparse PSD matrices as sums of clique-supported PSD components.

knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Space Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Chordal positive-semidefinite completion through maximal-clique principal submatrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be chordal, with maximal cliques \(C_1,\ldots,C_q\), and let \(X\) be a symmetric partial matrix whose specified entries are the diagonal and edges of \(G\). Then \(X\) admits a completion \(\widehat X\succeq0\) if and only if \[E_kXE_k^{\mathsf T}\succeq0\quad(k=1,\ldots,q),\] where \(E_k\) selects the indices in \(C_k\). Thus a domain-space SDP constraint on a chordally sparse partial matrix is represented by clique PSD constraints, together with agreement of any duplicated entries shared by different clique variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A chordal partial matrix has a positive-semidefinite completion exactly when every maximal-clique principal submatrix is positive semidefinite, with duplicated overlap entries identified.

knowledge_statements.title: Range-Space Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clique-sum representation of the sparse positive-semidefinite cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be chordal with maximal cliques \(C_1,\ldots,C_q\). The decomposition need not be unique when maximal cliques overlap.

knowledge_statements.title: Separator-Consistency Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistency equations for clique variables arranged by a running-intersection tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be a clique tree on maximal cliques \(C_k\), and assign a symmetric variable \(X_k\) to each clique. For every tree edge \(e=(k,\ell)\), let \(S_e=C_k\cap C_\ell\) and let \(R_{ke}\) select \(S_e\) from \(C_k\). The separator-consistency equations are \[R_{ke}X_kR_{ke}^{\mathsf T}=R_{\ell e}X_\ell R_{\ell e}^{\mathsf T}\quad(e\in E(T)).\] Under the running-intersection property, these edge equations are equivalent to agreement of all clique copies of every shared matrix entry and therefore define a single global partial matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a clique tree, equating the two copies of every separator submatrix is sufficient to make all overlapping clique matrices globally consistent.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) satisfies the running-intersection property.
\(X_k\) is symmetric and indexed by \(C_k\).
